extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys and agents practicing before the USPTO; lawyers and staff involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO (ALJ and Director/OED) to evaluate practitioner misconduct, determine violations of the USPTO disciplinary rules, and select appropriate sanctions and remedies (suspension, restitution, dissociation, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(3) - misappropriation/failure to remit client funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Misappropriation of, or failure to properly or timely remit, funds received by a practitioner or the practitioner's firm from a client to pay a fee which the client is required by law to pay to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: receiving client funds for USPTO filing fees but repeatedly submitting a debit card that is declined and not ensuring payment, resulting in abandonment. Such conduct falls within §10.23(c)(3) and constitutes disreputable/gross misconduct; may support suspension and restitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4) - dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes knowingly providing a form of payment that will be declined, falsely blaming the bank without corroborating evidence, or intentionally misleading a client about the status of an application. Credibility and objective evidence (bank records) are critical to rebut allegations of dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5) - conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that undermines the office process (e.g., neglect leading to abandonment of a patent application) can be prejudicial to the administration of justice and supports disciplinary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) - neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes neglect of a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to timely remit required fees or to respond to Office actions such that a client's application becomes abandoned is neglect under §10.77(c) and can justify suspension/exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) - conduct reflecting adversely on fitness to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad catchall for conduct showing unfitness (e.g., failing to cooperate with investigative requests, misrepresentations). Can be charged in addition to specific rules and supports sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and client communication (keep client informed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep clients informed of material developments (e.g., Notices to File Missing Parts, Notices of Incomplete Reply, Notice of Abandonment) and must not misrepresent the status of a client's matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to notify a client that filing fees were not paid or that an application went abandoned — or affirmatively misrepresenting that the application is 'still on track' — is professional misconduct and a basis for discipline and restitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate with OED investigations and produce records
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must respond to Requests for Information (RFIs), interrogatories, and discovery by OED and must produce requested documentation (e.g., bank statements) related to client funds and payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to produce bank records or to timely respond to RFIs/interrogatories is an aggravating factor. Misidentifying banks or producing incomplete records undermines credibility and supports adverse inferences and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing discipline, the decisionmaker must consider: (1) the nature, extent, and seriousness of the misconduct; (2) whether the misconduct was intentional; (3) the actual injury or potential injury caused by the misconduct; and (4) the existence of aggravating and mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors noted in the Order include lack of cooperation and lack of remorse; mitigating factors may include remediation/refunds. The Order cites ABA Standards and case precedent in weighing these factors. Multiple violations and intentional conduct support more severe sanctions (e.g., multi-year suspension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution and monetary remedies (37 C.F.R. § 11.20(b) guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may require restitution to persons financially injured by the practitioner's conduct or to an appropriate client's security trust fund as a condition of probation or reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restitution amount is based on actual measurable financial injury (example in this case: additional USPTO revival fees and surcharge of $945 + $65 = $1,010) minus any refunds already paid by the practitioner. Restitution may be imposed even if practitioner claims not to have charged legal fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and appellate-brief requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from an ALJ initial decision to the USPTO Director must be filed within 30 days and include an appellate brief that complies with §11.55 (clear statement of disputed facts and law; statement of issues on appeal; argument with citations; formatting requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A nonconforming or perfunctory brief may be refused entry and serves as an independent basis to deny the appeal. Arguments not raised at the hearing generally cannot be raised for the first time on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of professional rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20 et seq. and 11.101 et seq.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are subject to the USPTO Code of Professional Responsibility (37 C.F.R. §§ 10.20‑10.112) and/or the Rules of Professional Conduct (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101‑11.901), depending on timing of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misconduct is evaluated under the applicable rules in force at the time of the conduct (both sets may apply if conduct spans the rule-change date). Violations of these rules constitute grounds for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disreputable or gross misconduct standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Disreputable or gross misconduct is conduct violative of the ordinary standard of professional obligation and honor; disciplinary rules establish a professional floor below which a practitioner can be disciplined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court and USPTO precedent interpret this phrase broadly to include unprofessional conduct that undermines professional obligations; violation of a disciplinary rule necessarily constitutes disreputable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards, ALJ factfinding, and appellate scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The ALJ weighs evidence, resolves material conflicts, makes inferences, and issues findings of fact; on Director review the record may be reviewed de novo but substantial evidence supporting ALJ findings is controlling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable inferences by the ALJ (e.g., inferring a bank-excuse where no corroborating records provided) are afforded deference; issues not raised at hearing may be forfeited on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowing/intentional conduct as an aggravating element
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentional or knowing conduct (e.g., knowingly authorizing payments that one knows will be declined, intentionally withholding information from a client) is an aggravating factor that supports harsher sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order finds intentionality where practitioner failed to produce records and evidence contradicted his assertions. Intent increases likelihood of suspension/exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual injury as a sanction factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary review considers whether the practitioner's misconduct caused actual financial or other injury to the client (e.g., client had to pay revival fees because of abandonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual injury (measurable financial loss) supports restitution and more severe sanctions; examples include additional USPTO fees and surcharges the client incurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions and ancillary orders available to protect the public
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may impose suspension, exclusion, restitution, public notice to state disciplinary agencies and courts, dissociation from Customer Numbers and PKI certificates, prohibitions on obtaining Customer Numbers, and conditions for reinstatement (e.g., compliance with §11.58).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can include administrative steps to prevent further practice before the Office (dissociation of PKI/customer numbers) and conditions that must be satisfied before the practitioner may resume practice (payment of restitution, compliance with duties of disciplined practitioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping obligation for client funds and related proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner is expected to maintain sufficient financial records (bank statements, account numbers, records linking debit/credit card transactions to accounts) to substantiate payments and handling of client funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to maintain or produce these records when requested jeopardizes the practitioner's credibility and can lead to adverse inferences and discipline; producing incomplete or redacted records is insufficient.
